subject: Environment
topic: Forest Conservation Act and amendments — mixed tiers
description: Forest Conservation Act 1980, FRA 2006, CAMPA, Net Present Value, recent amendments

questions.stem: The Forest Conservation Act of India was enacted in:

options.option_text: 1980 (during Indira Gandhi's term)

questions.explanation: Forest (Conservation) Act, 1980 — restricts diversion of forest land for non-forestry purposes; needs Central Govt approval. Replaced earlier laissez-faire approach. Wildlife Protection Act — 1972. Environment Protection Act — 1986 (post-Bhopal). Forest Rights Act — 2006 (recognises tribal community rights over forest produce). FCA renamed in August 2023 to 'Van (Sanrakshan Evam Samvardhan) Adhiniyam' via the FCA (Amendment) Act 2023 — controversial, exempts certain border-area forests.

questions.stem: The Forest Rights Act, 2006 (Scheduled Tribes and Other Traditional Forest Dwellers Act) primarily seeks to:

options.option_text: Privatise all forest land
Recognise individual + community rights of forest-dwelling Scheduled Tribes and OTFDs over forest resources
Ban entry of all humans into forests
Convert forests into agriculture

questions.explanation: FRA 2006 — corrects 'historical injustice' to forest dwellers excluded from earlier forest laws. Recognises individual rights (4 ha cultivation), community rights (collection of MFP — non-timber forest produce), habitat rights (PVTGs), grazing rights. Gram Sabha is the key authority for verifying claims. Forest Rights Committee at village level. Implementation has lagged — many states reject claims; Niyamgiri verdict (2013) was a landmark FRA win for the Dongria Kondh tribe.

questions.stem: CAMPA (Compensatory Afforestation Fund Management and Planning Authority) collects funds for:

options.option_text: Conservation of marine ecosystems only
Compensatory afforestation when forest land is diverted for non-forestry use
Wildlife protection only
Climate change research

questions.explanation: CAMPA — established by Supreme Court order 2002, statutory under CAF Act 2016. When forest land is diverted under FCA (e.g., a road, mine, dam), the user agency must pay (a) Net Present Value of the lost forest + (b) cost of compensatory afforestation on equivalent non-forest land or twice degraded forest land. Funds go to a National CAMPA + State CAMPA. ~₹1 lakh crore accumulated; CAG critiqued slow utilisation. In 2024, MoEFCC issued new compensatory afforestation rules.

questions.stem: Total forest cover of India (per ISFR 2023 by FSI) is approximately:

options.option_text: 10% of geographical area
21-22% of geographical area (~7.15 lakh km²)
33% of geographical area (national policy goal)

questions.explanation: India State of Forest Report (ISFR) by Forest Survey of India (FSI), Dehradun — biennial since 1987. ISFR 2023: forest cover ~7.16 lakh km² = 21.76% of geographical area. Tree cover adds another ~3% → total green cover ~24.6%. National Forest Policy 1988 target — 33% (greater for hill regions). Top states by area: MP, Arunachal, Chhattisgarh, Odisha, Maharashtra. By percentage: Mizoram, Nagaland, Lakshadweep, Andamans (>80%). Mangrove cover ~4,991 km² (Sundarbans dominant).

questions.stem: The 'Joint Forest Management' (JFM) approach in India involves:

options.option_text: Forest land owned only by private companies
Local communities and forest department co-managing forest resources, sharing benefits
Foreign investment in forests
Total ban on tribal access

questions.explanation: JFM — formalised by NFP 1988 + 1990 Government Order. Forest department + Village Forest Committee jointly protect / develop a degraded forest patch — VFC gets share of MFP, fuelwood, fodder + part of timber revenue when matured. ~1.18 lakh JFM Committees in India by 2024. Critiqued: top-down, low community share, weak in non-degraded forests. FRA 2006 was a more rights-based approach, complementary to JFM.

questions.stem: The 'Wildlife Protection Act' 1972 has SIX schedules. Tigers, lions and other most-protected species fall under:

options.option_text: Schedule III
Schedule I (highest level of protection — penalties up to 7 years)
Schedule V (vermin)
Schedule VI (protected plants)

questions.explanation: WLPA 1972 (amended 2022) — Schedule I has the highest level of protection (highest penalties — up to 7 years, fines, no bail). Tigers, lions, snow leopards, GIBs, hangul, dolphin etc. Schedule II — moderate protection (e.g., assamese macaque). Schedule III — animals like sambar, chital. Schedule IV — partridges. Schedule V — VERMIN (rats, common crow, fruit bat — can be hunted). Schedule VI — endemic protected plants (orchids etc). 2022 amendments simplified Schedule numbers (now I-IV + plant schedule).

questions.stem: The 'Project Tiger' was launched at Jim Corbett National Park (Uttarakhand) on:

options.option_text: 1 January 1980
1 April 1973
26 January 1990
5 June 1992

questions.explanation: Project Tiger — launched 1 April 1973 by PM Indira Gandhi at Jim Corbett (then Hailey) National Park. Original 9 tiger reserves: Corbett, Manas, Ranthambore, Palamau, Sariska, Kanha, Melghat, Bandipur, Sunderbans. Now 58 tiger reserves (Mar 2025), the latest being Madhav (MP, 2024). Tiger census 2022 — 3,167 (up from 1,411 in 2006 nadir). NTCA (National Tiger Conservation Authority) is the statutory body (created 2006).

questions.stem: Under Section 2 of the Forest Conservation Act, 1980, which of the following activities requires prior approval of the Central Government?

options.option_text: Construction of forest rest houses for wildlife officials
Seasonal grazing by nomadic communities in buffer zones
Diversion of forest land for a road or a railway line
Patrolling tracks laid inside a reserved forest for fire lines

questions.explanation: Section 2 of FCA 1980 prohibits use of forest land for any 'non-forest purpose' without prior Central Government approval. Roads and railways are classic non-forest purposes. Fire lines, patrolling tracks, check-posts, and wildlife infrastructure are explicitly carved out as ancillary to forest management and do not require approval. Grazing under customary rights is also not classified as non-forest use.

questions.stem: The National Forest Policy, 1988 recommends maintaining forest and tree cover over what share of India's total geographical area to sustain ecological balance?

options.option_text: 20% of total geographical area of India
25% of total geographical area of India
33% of total geographical area of India
40% of total geographical area of India

questions.explanation: The National Forest Policy, 1988 sets a target of 33% (one-third) of India's geographical area under forest and tree cover — two-thirds for hill and mountainous regions and one-third for plains. The earlier 1952 Policy had recommended 60% cover for hills but was less specific about plains. 25% is a common distractor but is not the official target.

questions.stem: Which Supreme Court case extended the applicability of the Forest Conservation Act, 1980 to ALL forests — including unnotified ones — based on the dictionary meaning of the word 'forest'?

options.option_text: M.C. Mehta vs Union of India (1987), Oleum gas leak case
T.N. Godavarman Thirumulpad vs Union of India (1996)
Rural Litigation and Entitlement Kendra vs State of UP (1987)
Vellore Citizens Welfare Forum vs Union of India (1996)

questions.explanation: In the Godavarman case (1996), the Supreme Court ruled that FCA applies to ALL forests — irrespective of ownership or notification under Indian Forest Act 1927 — using the dictionary meaning of 'forest.' This dramatically expanded its scope to 'deemed forests.' M.C. Mehta (Oleum gas) and Vellore (tannery pollution) dealt with industrial pollution under EPA. The RLEK case covered Mussoorie limestone quarries.

questions.stem: The Forest Conservation Act, 1980 defines 'non-forest purpose.' Which of the following is EXPLICITLY EXCLUDED from that definition and therefore does NOT require Central Government approval?

options.option_text: Mining and coal extraction from forest land areas
Construction of highways and national roads in forests
Reforestation and afforestation activities on forest land
Setting up defence installations inside reserved forests

questions.explanation: The Explanation to Section 2 of FCA 1980 explicitly states that 'non-forest purpose' does NOT include work 'relating or ancillary to conservation, development and management of forests' — and specifically excludes afforestation and reforestation. Mining, roads, and defence installations are all non-forest purposes requiring prior Central Govt approval. Cultivation of tea, rubber, and spices is also treated as non-forest use under the Act.

questions.stem: Which statutory body is mandated under the Forest Conservation Rules to examine and advise the Central Government on proposals for diversion of forest land for non-forest purposes?

options.option_text: National Board for Wildlife (NBWL) at the Centre
Forest Advisory Committee (FAC) under MoEFCC
Central Empowered Committee (CEC) of the Supreme Court
National Green Tribunal (NGT) environmental review bench

questions.explanation: Rule 3 of the Forest Conservation Rules mandates that proposals for diversion of forest land be referred to the Forest Advisory Committee (FAC) constituted by MoEFCC. FAC comprises the Director General of Forests and domain experts. NBWL specifically covers wildlife-affected areas; CEC is a Supreme Court-appointed body for compliance monitoring, not a statutory advisory body under FCA; NGT adjudicates disputes but does not advise on diversion proposals.

questions.stem: The Forest (Conservation) Amendment Act, 2023 introduced an exemption from prior Central Government approval for security-related infrastructure on forest land located within what distance from India's international borders or Line of Control?

options.option_text: 50 kilometres from any international border of India
75 kilometres from international borders in NE states only
100 kilometres from international borders or Line of Control
25 kilometres from the Line of Actual Control only

questions.explanation: The 2023 Amendment Act (renamed Van Sanrakshan Evam Samvardhan Adhiniyam) carved out an exemption for security and border infrastructure on forest land within 100 km of international borders or the LoC, subject to a ceiling of 10 hectares per project without prior approval. This was contentious because large forest tracts in Arunachal Pradesh, Sikkim, and Uttarakhand fall within this zone. The 50/75/25 km figures are distractors; the Act uniformly applies the 100 km threshold.

questions.stem: The Forest (Conservation) Amendment Act, 2023 restricted the definition of 'forest land' under FCA to officially recorded and notified categories, effectively reversing a landmark judicial expansion of forest protection established through which mechanism?

options.option_text: National Forest Policy 1988 administrative guidelines
1996 Supreme Court interpretation in the Godavarman case
Environment Protection Act 1986 notifications on forest areas
Biological Diversity Act 2002 definitions of biodiversity-rich land

questions.explanation: The Godavarman judgment (1996) had extended FCA to ALL forests by dictionary meaning, including unnotified 'deemed forests.' The 2023 Amendment restricted 'forest land' to: (i) reserved/protected forests under the Indian Forest Act 1927, (ii) land recorded as forest in government records on or after 25 Oct 1980, and (iii) land covered by prior FCA diversion orders. This excluded vast unrecorded 'deemed forests' that Godavarman had protected. The National Forest Policy and EPA notifications have no definitional authority over FCA scope.
